summary.value: The Icelandic chicken is a landrace that Norse settlers carried to Iceland around a thousand years ago. For centuries it was the only chicken on the island, chosen for thrift and good mothering rather than for looks, so there is no fixed standard. A flock shows almost every color and pattern, several comb types, and some birds wear a small crest, but true Icelandics never have feathered legs. They are small birds: cocks weigh about 4.5 to 5.25 pounds and hens 3 to 3.5. Hens lay around 180 white to cream eggs a year, small to medium in size, and keep laying through winter. Many hens go broody and raise their own chicks. The birds are lively and curious, turn friendly when handled young, fly well and forage hard. They are very hardy in cold, harsh weather and suit free range homesteads and beginners, though not a closed pen.
